record.original_question: Let A352991 be the OEIS sequence obtained by listing, in increasing order, all decimal concatenations coming from distinct permutations of the first m positive integers for varying m. If a term A352991(n) is a perfect power and is greater than 1, must it always be a perfect square and never a higher-order perfect power c^k with k >= 3? Equivalently, are there no nontrivial cubes, fourth powers, or other higher perfect powers anywhere in A352991?

evidence.quote: Definition 2.3. We define the OEIS sequence A352991 as the concatenation of all the distinct permutations of the first strictly positive m integers, sorted in ascending order (e.g., 12345671089 is a term of the sequence, while 12345670189 does not belong to A352991, even if all the digits of the string 1 2 3 . . . 9 10 appear once and only once, since '10' is missed).

Conjecture 3.1. Let n in N - {0, 1} be given. We (provocatively) conjecture that if n is such that A352991(n) is a perfect power of an integer, then there does not exist k in N - {0, 1, 2} such that A352991(n) = c^k, c in N.

Remark 3.1. If confirmed, Conjecture 3.1 would imply that all the perfect powers (strictly greater than 1) in A352991 are perfect squares and nothing more (no cube, no square of square, and so forth).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For each integer $m\ge 1$, consider all permutations $(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_m)$ of the set $\{1,2,\dots,m\}$, and form the decimal concatenation $\overline{a_1 a_2 \cdots a_m}$ obtained by writing each $a_i$ in base $10$ (without leading zeros) one after another. Let $S$ be the set of all positive integers obtained in this way as $m$ ranges over $\mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}$ and the permutation ranges over all $m!$ permutations of $\{1,\dots,m\}$. Arrange $S$ in strictly increasing order as a sequence $s_1<s_2<s_3<\cdots$.

Prove or disprove: for every $n\ge 2$ such that $s_n>1$ is a perfect power (i.e., $s_n=c^k$ for some integers $c\ge 2$ and $k\ge 2$), one must have $k=2$. Equivalently, show that the sequence $(s_n)$ contains no integer of the form $c^k$ with $c\ge 2$ and $k\ge 3$.
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture remains open. It has been verified computationally for all terms below 10111121314151617181920212223456789 with no counterexample, and a partial theoretical result rules out perfect powers when m ≡ 2, 3, 5, 6 (mod 9), but no full proof or disproof is known.

status_evidence.title: On some open problems concerning perfect powers (arXiv HTML)
status_evidence.snippet: This challenging conjecture has been checked for any integer smaller than 10111121314151617181920212223456789 and no counterexample has been found so far.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is stated as open and only computationally verified up to a large bound.

status_evidence.title: A001597 - OEIS (perfect powers)
status_evidence.snippet: Reference to the conjecture on A352991 regarding higher perfect powers.
status_evidence.claim: OEIS references confirm the conjecture is current and unresolved.
